stumbles.quote: Remex's hash cells hold 70% of true neighbours while scanning 34%.
stumbles.why: Remex is never explained, nor are its "hash cells" (what hash, how cells are formed). The baseline is unclear.
Refers to earlier work between Oskar and the author that the text never describes. A reader can't tell what it is.
Oskar and e-means are never introduced. The text doesn't say what e-means is or how it differs from Lloyd's k-means.

stumbles.quote: I expected the payoff to be offset coding and treated the index cells as a side note. The results came out the other way.
stumbles.why: Offset coding is used here before it is defined. It is only explained in a later paragraph.

stumbles.quote: Training speed is the gain the paper advertises.
stumbles.why: This seems to conflict with the heading's claim of 60x selectivity. The text never says which gain the heading refers to, or why the selectivity result is e-means-specific when Lloyd gives the same recall.

stumbles.quote: 1 to 3 passes. On 4 CPUs that is 1.6 to 10.2 times sooner.
stumbles.why: The mapping from 1–3 passes to the 1.6–10.2x speedup is unexplained. It isn't clear what the range depends on, or whether a pass is comparable to a Lloyd iteration.

stumbles.quote: The centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector at 100,000 vectors, though.
stumbles.why: The figure is not derived. 4,096 centroids × 768 dims × 4 bytes ÷ 100,000 is about 126, but the text never gives the dimension or float width. "Per vector" amortization is not explained.

stumbles.quote: A second bit per dimension costs less than that.
stumbles.why: No cost is given for the second bit, so the comparison can't be checked. The recall it buys is also not stated.

stumbles.quote: The centroids are more useful for routing queries than for coding vectors.
stumbles.why: The 60x figure is never derived. 34% / 0.56% is about 61, but the two recall levels differ (90% vs 70%), so the comparison isn't like for like. The text also never describes how queries are routed, such as how many cells are probed.

point: Using e-means or Lloyd centroids as index cells in remex scans far less of the corpus for good recall (90% at 0.56% vs 70% at 34%), which makes that a better use of them than offset coding, and the author plans to adopt them.
